title: Acute Kidney Injury as a Marker of Disease Severity and In-Hospital Mortality Among Malaria Patients in Luanda, Angola
content: Background: Malaria remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent complication of severe malaria and poor clinical outcomes. However, data integrating parasitemia, renal dysfunction, hematological parameters, and in-hospital mortality among malaria patients in Angola remain limited. Objective: To evaluate AKI as a marker of disease severity and in-hospital mortality among patients hospitalized with malaria in Luanda, Angola, with particular emphasis on its association with parasite burden, renal biochemical parameters, and hematological characteristics. Methods: A hospital-based observational study was conducted among 400 patients aged 12–66 years hospitalized with malaria at Josina Machel Hospital, Luanda, Angola, from March to August 2023. Patients were classified according to the presence of AKI based on serum creatinine using KDIGO criteria. Results: Of the 400 participants, 247 had no AKI and 153 had AKI. Patients with AKI had higher mean parasite density than those without AKI (2088 ± 4061.8 vs. 1293.3 ± 2171.2 parasites/mm³; p = 0.011). Serum urea and creatinine were higher in the AKI group (72.1 ± 49.9 vs. 34.9 ± 27.6 mg/dL and 3.4 ± 2.6 vs. 0.72 ± 0.30 mg/dL, respectively; both p < 0.001), while eGFR was substantially lower (37.9 ± 20.5 vs. 170.9 ± 74.7 mL/min/1.73 m²; p < 0.001). MCV and MCH were higher among patients with AKI (p<0.05), whereas hemoglobin, RBC count, RDW, and MCHC did not differ significantly (p>0.05). In-hospital mortality was higher among patients with AKI than among those without AKI (15.7% vs. 0.8%; p < 0.001). AKI was associated with in-hospital death (OR: 25.6, 95% CI: 5.80–113). Conclusion: AKI was associated with higher parasite burden, substantial renal dysfunction, and increased in-hospital mortality among hospitalized malaria patients. These findings support AKI as an important marker of disease severity and poor prognosis in malaria. Early assessment and monitoring of renal function may help identify patients at risk of clinical deterioration and death in hospital. Further prospective studies are warranted to determine the independent prognostic value of AKI in malaria.
